opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting framing, and I'd say we're closer than many people assume, but it might not look the way people expect.

With Move 37, there was a clean, objective signal: you play the game out and you see whether the move was brilliant. Healthcare doesn't have that. Feedback loops are long, outcomes are noisy, and there often isn't a single right answer. So even if a model made a genuinely superhuman call, it might be hard to recognize it as such in the moment.

That said, there are hints already. We've seen models pick up signals in medical images that clinicians didn't know were there, like predicting things from retinal scans or ECGs that weren't thought to be visible in that data. And in diagnostic reasoning, models increasingly surface differentials that a busy clinician might not consider, especially for rare conditions. Those aren't quite Move 37 yet, but they rhyme with it.

I think the bigger Move 37 moments will come in places where we can close the loop: drug discovery, protein design, maybe treatment selection where we can run trials and see the result. There, a model might propose something that looks strange to experts and then turns out to work.

On the clinical side, I'd expect it to be more gradual. It'll be less one stunning move and more the accumulation of cases where the model noticed something the care team missed. Eventually we'll look back and realize that, in aggregate, it was making calls humans wouldn't have.

The other piece is that we have to build the evaluation and trust infrastructure to recognize those moments. If a model says something surprising, is it a hallucination or an insight? Getting good at telling those apart, through better evals, better uncertainty estimates, and careful human-AI collaboration, is what will let us actually benefit from a Move 37 rather than dismissing it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we're closer than people assume in some narrow places, and further than the hype suggests in the way that actually matters.

If you define Move 37 as a prediction a human wouldn't have made, we've arguably already seen flashes of it. Models can look at a retinal image and infer cardiovascular risk factors, or predict sex from a fundus photo, which ophthalmologists had no idea was even possible. Those are genuinely surprising, superhuman signals that no clinician was trained to see. In that sense, the "brilliant prediction" part has happened.

But the thing that made Move 37 special wasn't just that it was surprising. It was that it was surprising, correct, and legible after the fact. Experts initially thought it was a mistake, then watched the game unfold and realized it was deep. In healthcare, that second step is the hard part. If a model says "this patient will deteriorate in 48 hours" and the care team can't see why, they're not going to act on it, and honestly they shouldn't blindly. Medicine is a domain where you have to earn the right to be trusted on a surprising call, because the downside of a confident wrong answer is a person, not a lost game.

So the real bottleneck isn't raw capability. Models are already good enough to find patterns humans miss. The bottleneck is building the surrounding system: calibration, so the model knows when it's uncertain; explanation or at least evidence, so a clinician can interrogate the reasoning; and evaluation in realistic settings rather than benchmark exams. When we worked on things like Med-PaLM, the part that kept me humble wasn't the exam scores, it was how differently a system behaves when a real patient types a messy, ambiguous question with missing context.

My honest guess is that we'll get Move 37 moments at the level of individual signals, in imaging and in multimodal prediction, in the next few years, and in some cases we already have. The Move 37 moment at the level of a whole diagnostic reasoning chain, where a model says something non-obvious about a patient, a physician initially disagrees, and the model turns out to be right in a way that changes practice, I think that's further out, maybe not because of the model but because we don't yet have the infrastructure to notice it, verify it, and let it propagate.

The thing I'd want people to take away is that the exciting version of this isn't AI beating doctors. It's AI and clinicians together getting to answers neither would reach alone, and building the trust layer so that when the surprising prediction comes, we actually listen.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re closer to making a surprising prediction than we are to knowing that it’s a brilliant one. That distinction matters a lot in healthcare.

With Move 37, there were clear rules and, ultimately, an outcome that helped establish the value of the move. In medicine, if a model suggests something that no physician would have considered, that could be a profound insight—or it could just be wrong. And the feedback can take months or years, with all sorts of confounding factors.

So I’d look for this first in a narrower setting: a model noticing a pattern in a patient’s history, suggesting an unexpected diagnosis, and then having that diagnosis confirmed by a test. That’s a setting where you can close the loop and establish that the surprising insight was useful.

I’m optimistic about that. But the milestone I care about is whether those insights reliably improve patient outcomes. Getting there requires both capable models and a really good process for testing what they discover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re probably closer to seeing something that looks like a Move 37 than we are to knowing that it really is one. A model can make a surprising recommendation today. The hard part is establishing that it’s correct—that it improves outcomes, rather than just sounding clever.

And healthcare is different from Go in a really important way: we don’t have a clean reward signal at the end of every game. Patients are different, outcomes take time, and you often don’t get to observe what would have happened if you’d made a different decision.

So I’d look for this first in a setting where you can test the prediction rigorously. Maybe a model spots a pattern that leads to an unexpected diagnosis, or identifies a treatment hypothesis that people hadn’t considered. Then you validate it. That loop—from surprising suggestion to convincing evidence—is what would make it a real Move 37 moment for me.
